question:
Patient note:
A 52-year-old woman is reviewed this morning in the ambulatory procedure area just before transfer to the minor-surgery suite, where the hand team plans a limited open release of a long-standing right carpal-tunnel stenosis; the surgeon anticipates a 25-minute skin-to-skin time under a regional axillary block with monitored anesthesia care and same-day discharge once motor function returns. She arrived unassisted from the parking structure, climbed two flights of stairs without stopping, and states she remains able to complete her usual afternoon two-mile neighborhood walk, though she admits her calves feel “heavy” by evening and shoe straps leave impressions around both ankles. Inspection confirms rope-like, tortuous superficial veins coursing along the medial aspects of both lower legs, and there is 1–2 + pitting edema to mid-shin that indents with thumb pressure yet resolves after overnight elevation. She recalls first noticing the dilated veins in her twenties when she worked retail shifts on concrete floors; no duplex studies have ever demonstrated clot, and she has never experienced sudden calf tenderness, pleuritic chest pain, or a radiologist-confirmed pulmonary embolus. Electronic records reveal no prior femoral, jugular, or implanted ports, and today the only access is a single 20-gauge peripheral catheter placed by nursing in the left antecubital fossa that flushes easily; she has never carried a tunneled line or peripherally inserted central catheter. One notable complication in her chart is an episode of immune-mediated thrombocytopenia that developed eight years ago after a prolonged postoperative infusion of unfractionated heparin for cesarean-section prophylaxis: platelets fell from 240 × 10⁹ L⁻¹ to 50 × 10⁹ L⁻¹ within five days, a serotonin-release assay returned strongly positive, and counts rebounded promptly once the heparin was stopped and argatroban substituted; she was counseled thereafter to avoid all forms of heparin and carries a wallet card alerting clinicians to that history. Three weeks ago she awoke with crushing substernal discomfort radiating to the left shoulder; emergency crews documented ST-segment elevations in leads V2–V5, and coronary angiography revealed a thrombotic occlusion of the proximal left anterior descending artery that was treated with drug-eluting stent placement. She completed an uneventful two-day coronary-care stay, now takes ticagrelor and low-dose aspirin that were paused after cardiology consultation 24 hours ago to reduce procedural bleeding, and reports no recurrent chest tightness, orthopnea, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Aside from essential hypertension managed with lisinopril 10 mg each morning and hyperlipidemia treated with nightly rosuvastatin 20 mg, she denies chronic heart-failure admissions, recent febrile illnesses, systemic infections, or lung infiltrates; a chest radiograph obtained last week at follow-up demonstrated clear fields and stable cardiac silhouette. She has never needed casts, braces, or traction devices and has avoided high-energy trauma or long-bone fractures. There is no personal or first-degree family history of unexplained clots, strokes, inflammatory bowel disease, connective-tissue disorders, or inherited procoagulant mutations, and genetic testing for factor V Leiden or the prothrombin G20210A variant has never been pursued. During a hematology follow-up visit last year, however, she underwent a comprehensive thrombophilia screen that confirmed absence of factor V Leiden and prothrombin G20210A mutations and showed a negative lupus anticoagulant. She quit smoking 15 years ago after a 10-pack-year exposure, drinks a glass of red wine on weekends, and her body-mass index at pre-operative check-in is 27 kg m⁻². Vital signs ten minutes ago: temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 122/76 mm Hg, heart rate 68 beats min⁻¹ in regular rhythm, respiratory rate 14 min⁻¹, and oxygen saturation 97 % on room air. Airway evaluation shows Mallampati class II, normal dentition, and full cervical extension. Jugular venous pressure is below the sternal angle, the point of maximal impulse is nondisplaced, S₁ and S₂ are crisp without murmurs or gallops, and lungs are clear to auscultation with symmetrical excursion. The abdomen is soft and non-tender with active bowel sounds; no organomegaly is appreciated. Peripheral pulses are 2 + in dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries, and calf circumferences measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosities are 38 cm bilaterally without asymmetry. Neurologic screening reveals full orientation, intact cranial nerves, and 5/5 strength in all major muscle groups. Morning laboratory studies drawn from the peripheral line show hemoglobin 13.9 g dL⁻¹, hematocrit 41 %, platelets 236 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, leukocytes 6.8 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, sodium 139 mmol L⁻¹, potassium 4.1 mmol L⁻¹, bicarbonate 24 mmol L⁻¹, creatinine 0.92 mg dL⁻¹, AST 24 U L⁻¹, ALT 21 U L⁻¹, total bilirubin 0.7 mg dL⁻¹, prothrombin time 11.9 s with an international normalized ratio of 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 30 s. A 12-lead electrocardiogram reviewed by anesthesia displays normal sinus rhythm at 66 beats min⁻¹ with well-formed Q waves in V2–V4 consistent with the recent infarction but no acute ST-T changes. Sequential compression sleeves have been fitted around both calves yet remain inactive until draping is complete; pharmacologic prophylaxis has been deferred because of the prior antibody-mediated reaction, and the hematology service is on standby to recommend a direct thrombin inhibitor should unplanned systemic anticoagulation become necessary during the case. She has been nil per os since midnight, has voided recently, and consents to proceed after risks, benefits, and alternatives are discussed.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini VTE score sums weighted perioperative risk factors.
• Age 52 (41–60 years): 1 point.
• Planned 25-minute carpal-tunnel release (minor surgery under 45 minutes): 1 point.
• BMI 27 kg/m² (>25): 1 point.
• Visible varicose veins: 1 point.
• Current swollen legs (bilateral pitting edema): 1 point, separate from varicose veins.
• Myocardial infarction 3 weeks ago (within 1 month): 1 point.
• Prior confirmed heparin-induced thrombocytopenia: 3 points, even though the platelet count is now normal.
She is ambulatory, has no history of DVT or PE, and has a peripheral IV rather than central venous access. These add no points.
Total = 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 3 = 9.
Final answer: 9
